sections.h2: Merchandise exports barely moved despite a roughly 10% weaker rupee

chart.title: Exports grew 0.93% while the rupee weakened about 10.4%

sections.means: Even without petroleum, export growth stayed far below what a 10% price advantage would be expected to buy.
sections.todo: Judge exchange-rate policy against export volumes, not against the headline rupee move alone.

sections.h2: Imported inputs absorb much of the rupee gain for most exporters

chart.title: Over half of exports come from industries that import heavily
chart.source: India Exim Bank, Occasional Paper No. 228 (2025).

sections.means: When the rupee falls, firms that import heavily see input costs rise almost as fast as their rupee revenue.
sections.todo: Trade-intensive firms should hedge and diversify input suppliers, as the Exim Bank's sectoral advice says.

sections.h2: Only food and agro gets the full textbook benefit from a weaker rupee

chart.title: Food and agro imports 8.7% of its raw material, far below the rest
chart.sub: Import intensity of raw material by sector, %.
chart.source: India Exim Bank, Occasional Paper No. 228 (2025).

sections.means: Sector import intensity runs from 8.7% in food and agro to 80% in petroleum, which sets each sector's currency exposure.
sections.todo: Trade-intensive sectors should hedge and diversify input suppliers before relying on a weaker rupee.

sections.h2: Demand moves Indian exports about four times as much as the exchange rate

chart.title: World GDP elasticity of 4.15 dwarfs the exchange-rate effect of 1.07
chart.sub: Long-run export elasticities in the Exim Bank's 2025 model.
chart.source: India Exim Bank, Occasional Paper No. 228 (2025).

sections.means: In the Exim Bank's own model, foreign demand matters far more to exports than the exchange rate does.
sections.todo: Exporters should push market access and buyer financing rather than rely on currency competitiveness alone.
